anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=137; printed_page=123; section="3.1.1 Model of Concepts Introduction / Table 3.1"

anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=138; printed_page=124; section="3.1.2 Capturing Classes and Their Relationships in a Model of Concepts"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: An attribute is a property of a class that represents an essential characteristic of the class.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Identify Generalizations
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=147; printed_page=133; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Identify Generalizations"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: Identify groups of classes that have a common substance. For these classes, define generalizations in the form of more generic classes that will carry common attributes and relationships.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Complete the Generalizations
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=148; printed_page=134; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Complete the Generalizations"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: For identified generalizations (identified generic classes), check that all their respective specializations are identified (complete). If not, identify the missing specializations.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Aggregations and Compositions
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=150; printed_page=136; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Aggregations and Compositions"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: Examine each association, and distinguish simple associations from aggregations. Analyze the individual aggregating classes, and determine all the classes that they may consist of. Distinguish whether instances of the classes that make up the aggregations can exist independently or not.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Aggregations and Compositions
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=151; printed_page=137; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Aggregations and Compositions"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: capture the relationship with them as aggregations; for those that cannot, capture the relationship as compositions.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Identify the Classes That Represent Roles
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=151; printed_page=137; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Identify the Classes That Represent Roles"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: Decide which of the identified classes represent roles of another class and stereotype them as ≪role≫. Always distinguish between role and actor. An actor (class) can act in different roles.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Identify the Classes That Represent Roles
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=152; printed_page=138; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Identify the Classes That Represent Roles"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: Each role can have (and usually does have) its own attributes, and even so, we keep the identity of the person acting in those roles in one place (the Person class); thus, there is no duplication of actor’s details.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Roles in Associations
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=155; printed_page=141; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Roles in Associations"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: To distinguish the roles, the role specification on the association should be used. If you find that the specified role has its own attributes, you need to capture it using the class (see above).

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Attributes
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=155; printed_page=141; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Attributes"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: For all classes, specify the relevant attributes and whether they are mandatory or optional.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Attributes
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=156; printed_page=142; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Attributes"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: All attributes representing the essential characteristics of the class for the business being modelled should be captured. Attribute obligation is captured through multiplicity: 1..1 indicates a mandatory attribute and 0..1 an optional one.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Operations
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=157; printed_page=143; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Operations"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: Class operations need to be specified based on some evidence, not just intuitively. The basic sources for specifying class operations are two models: the object life cycle model of the particular class and the model of the concepts itself.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Operations
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=157; printed_page=143; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Operations"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: If so, examine that model, and capture the operations listed in the state transitions as operations of that class in the model of concepts.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Operations
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=157; printed_page=143; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Operations"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: Examine the individual attributes and associations (including aggregations and compositions) of each class, and specify the operations that change their value.

anchors.section: 3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Operations
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=158; printed_page=144; section="3.1.4 How to Create a Model of Concepts > Specify Class Operations"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: Based on the relationship of the Delivery Order and the Package, we have specified operations addPackage() and removePackage(). The reason why there are two operations is because it is a 1:N relationship, and thus there must be operations that allow iterative addition and removal of container items.

anchors.section: 4.2 Consistency Evaluation
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=196; printed_page=182; section="4.2 Consistency Evaluation"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: If an inconsistency is found, it should be corrected to ensure the consistency of the business system model.

anchors.section: 4.2 Consistency Evaluation
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=196; printed_page=182; section="4.2 Consistency Evaluation"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: It is not a matter of aligning one model to the other (since both models may be incorrect), but to correct, one must first determine what are the facts (reality) and how they should be captured correctly and then correct the models accordingly.

anchors.section: 4.3.2 Process Map and the Process Flow Models Consistency
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=200; printed_page=186; section="4.3.2 Process Map and the Process Flow Models Consistency"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: Rule #2: The target state specified for a particular process in the process map is also specified in the process flow model of that process in the form of a specific object state set by the corresponding task of that process.

anchors.section: 4.4 Basic Temporal Consistency Rules
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=216; printed_page=202; section="4.4 Basic Temporal Consistency Rules"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: The other option is to do this evaluation is using so called consistency table, which structurally compares how consistently the temporal models (process flow models and object life cycle models) capture the succession (event/reason → action → resulting state) and whether they match each other (Table 4.2). If not, the models need to be adjusted to avoid inconsistencies.

anchors.section: 4.5.1 Process Flow and Object Life Cycle Models Consistency
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=219; printed_page=205; section="4.5.1 Process Flow and Object Life Cycle Models Consistency"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: Rule: For objects whose states are captured as alternatives in the process model, it is true that these states are also alternatives in their life cycle.

anchors.section: 4.5.1 Process Flow and Object Life Cycle Models Consistency
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=219; printed_page=205; section="4.5.1 Process Flow and Object Life Cycle Models Consistency"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: If the states of an object within a particular object life cycle model are alternative, these states need to be alternative in the process flow model too (Fig. 4.21).

anchors.section: 4.4 Basic Temporal Consistency Rules
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=219; printed_page=205; section="4.4 Basic Temporal Consistency Rules"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: If any of the recorded rows shows an inconsistency in the sequence event/reason → action → state, it is necessary to review the models and decide which model is right (if any) and which has to be changed so that the sequence is consistent in both models.

anchors.section: 4.5.2 Object Life Cycle Models and Model of Concepts Consistency
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=221; printed_page=207; section="4.5.2 Object Life Cycle Models and Model of Concepts Consistency"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: Rule #2: Each 1:N association in the model of concepts is reflected in an iterative cycle in the life cycle model of an object of that class.

anchors.section: 4.5.2 Object Life Cycle Models and Model of Concepts Consistency
anchors.sourceLocator: D1:physical_page=221; printed_page=207; section="4.5.2 Object Life Cycle Models and Model of Concepts Consistency"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: The creation and modification of a possible 1:N class relationship captured in the model of concepts must be captured in the object life cycle model of that class as state transitions that can be performed iteratively (Fig. 4.23).

anchors.sourceExcerpt: El Catálogo Madre está correctamente estructurado como inventario canónico versionado, no como flujo visible. La reducción a 40+20 debe ocurrir en runtime, no mediante eliminación editorial. Los nodos no visibles permanecen como derivaciones, aclaraciones, gaps, reglas, checkpoints o preparación VSM/AHE no diagnóstica.

anchors.section: 1. Decisión arquitectónica del catálogo runtime
anchors.sourceLocator: D7:section="1. Decisión arquitectónica del catálogo runtime"; paragraph_text_prefix="El nuevo catálogo no es una lista recortada de preguntas. Es una capa runtime co"
anchors.sourceExcerpt: El nuevo catálogo no es una lista recortada de preguntas. Es una capa runtime compuesta por interacciones visibles, confirmaciones asistidas, derivaciones internas, reglas de branching, gaps y salidas estructurales hacia MMABP. La unidad operativa visible se denomina Pregunta Runtime Compuesta y puede mapear a uno o varios Nodos Canónicos de Captura del Catálogo Madre.
